title: AI Is Making Verification the Bottleneck for Companies
content:
Summary.
Hierarchy does more than route information; it also verifies: deciding what information means, what deserves the firm’s attention, which outputs can be trusted, and which are worth
Somewhere in your company today, an expert rejected a perfectly plausible answer. A controller caught a revenue figure that counted deferred bookings. A security engineer blocked a release that passed every test but would have handed an AI agent write access to the production database. That override, escalation, or reversal is the most valuable data your firm produces. If you record enough of those moments and use them, alongside everything else your firm knows and measures, to train an AI model that learns from each correction, you could, in theory, eliminate the need for managers to route information and coordinate action. In doing so, execution gets turbocharged by automation. You might even be able to eliminate hierarchy altogether.

report.summary: As AI accelerates output, expert verification becomes the corporate bottleneck, and firms that capture corrections can train models to automate routing and oversight.
report.background: For decades, corporate hierarchy has done more than route information: managers and experts decide what data means, what deserves attention, and which outputs are trustworthy. Generative AI and agentic systems now produce plans, code, analyses, and decisions at volumes that overwhelm traditional review. The scarce resource is no longer drafting or analysis but verification by people with domain judgment. HBR argues that each expert override, escalation, or reversal contains valuable tacit knowledge. If companies systematically record those moments, with context and rationale, they can build datasets for evaluation, fine-tuning, and oversight automation. That could speed execution while preserving control, but it also raises governance, accountability, and data-quality questions.
key_points: AI shifts the bottleneck from production to verification. When models can generate plausible answers, code, and actions quickly, the limiting factor becomes expert review: deciding whether an output is correct, safe, and worth acting on. Organizations that treat review as an afterthought will accumulate risk and slow down.

Expert overrides are high-value training data. A controller catching deferred revenue or a security engineer blocking risky database access reveals tacit judgment that is rarely captured. Logging the context, rationale, and outcome of corrections can turn scattered reviews into a reusable dataset for evaluation and model improvement.

Correction data can enable a verification learning loop. Firms can use recorded overrides alongside existing metrics to train models that recognize risky outputs, route exceptions, and learn from each correction. Over time, this may automate parts of coordination and review, but only if data quality and feedback loops are strong.

Automating verification does not mean eliminating accountability. Even if models learn from expert corrections, firms still need audit trails, escalation paths, and clear ownership for high-stakes decisions. The article's vision of removing hierarchy is theoretically attractive but practically constrained by liability and governance.

The biggest implementation challenge is capturing judgment at scale. Reviewers must record why they intervened without adding excessive friction. Standardized taxonomies, lightweight capture tools, and privacy-aware data pipelines are needed before correction data can reliably train oversight systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, verification is becoming a product category: evaluation, observability, guardrails, and human-in-the-loop tooling will matter as much as model capability. Developers will need to design systems that log overrides, preserve rationale, and route uncertain outputs to experts rather than optimizing only for generation speed. For regular users, the shift could mean more reliable AI assistants and agents, but also more structured review and less seamless automation in high-stakes domains. Companies that master correction capture may gain a durable advantage; those that do not risk scaling plausible but unverified outputs. The article's deeper point is that AI does not remove hierarchy's judgment role automatically; it makes that role more explicit, measurable, and potentially automatable.
report.tools: Watch human-in-the-loop evaluation and correction-capture tools such as LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, Humanloop, and Label Studio; workflow orchestration tools like Temporal; and guardrail/eval frameworks such as Guardrails AI and OpenAI Evals. Start by logging overrides with context, outcome, and reviewer rationale, then build a labeled correction dataset before automating verification.
